evergreen_facts.text: Tokyo was called Edo until 1868, when it was renamed and became the seat of the emperor.
Edo, today's Tokyo, was the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate, which ruled Japan from 1603 to 1867.
The Great Kantō earthquake of 1923 and the fires that followed devastated Tokyo and nearby Yokohama.
Tokyo hosted the 1964 Summer Olympics, the first Olympic Games ever held in Asia.
Sensō-ji in Tokyo's Asakusa district is the city's oldest temple, traditionally founded in the year 645.
Tokyo's Meiji Shrine honors Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken and sits in a forest planted by volunteers.
Tokyo Tower, completed in 1958, is a lattice tower inspired by the Eiffel Tower and painted white and orange.
The Imperial Palace in central Tokyo stands on the grounds of the former Edo Castle.
The Kabuki-za theater in Tokyo's Ginza district is the city's principal stage for traditional kabuki drama.
A statue at Tokyo's Shibuya Station honors Hachikō, the Akita dog who waited there for his late owner for years.
Nigiri sushi, hand-pressed rice topped with fish, took its modern form in Edo, old Tokyo, in the early 1800s.
Monjayaki, a runny batter fried on a griddle and eaten straight off it, is a specialty of Tokyo's Tsukishima area.
Tokyo lies at the head of Tokyo Bay on the Kantō Plain, the largest plain in Japan.
Tokyo's territory includes the Ogasawara Islands, about 1,000 km to the south in the Pacific Ocean.
On clear days Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, can be seen from Tokyo about 100 km to the southwest.
Tokyo's Ueno Park, lined with cherry trees, is one of the city's best-loved spots for hanami, or blossom viewing.
